Abstract
We propose a forecast combination scheme that employs time-varying weights, which depend on the financial decision for 
which the forecasts are used. Combination weights are computed through three alternative economic performance meas-
ures, a utility-based function, an option staddle trading strategy, and a risk management loss function. We apply our model 
combination approach to various realized volatility estimators of the S&P500 and compare the forecasting performance of 
the combinations based on economic criteria to that of a variety of existing combination methods based on statistical loss 
functions. The results imply that our proposed combination schemes result to superior economic performance compared 
with the individual measures and statistical combination methods. Our findings are supported by a wide range of robustness 
checks and extensions Moreover, the suggested combination framework holds significant economic value during times of 
crisis and high volatility.

Introduction
Volatility forecasting plays a pivotal role in financial mar-
kets, making it a subject of great interest for researchers, 
traders, and investors. The ability to accurately anticipate 
and forecast volatility has significant implications for asset 
pricing, portfolio optimization, option pricing, hedging, and 
risk management. However, volatility forecasting is inher-
ently challenging due to the complex nature of financial mar-
kets and the presence of numerous unpredictable factors. 
Moreover, different models may perform differently under 
varying market conditions, making it essential to continu-
ally evaluate and update forecasting techniques to capture 
the evolving market environment. With the availability of 
high frequency data, a vast body of research has emerged in 
the context of the so-called realized volatility (RV), and a 
variety of RV measures have been proposed (see Andersen 
et al. 2010; Aït-Sahalia and Jacod 2014; for surveys on 
RV measures). Advancements in this field have led to the 
development of estimators that account for market micro-
structure effects, are applicable in multivariate settings, 
and can effectively handle jumps, leverage effect, and long 
memory in asset prices (see Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard 
2004; Zhang et al. 2005; Patton and Sheppard 2015 among 
others).
In this paper, we aim to explore the benefits of combining 
various RV measures on the basis of economic rather than 
solely statistical criteria. Our motivation for this approach 
is threefold. First, the field of financial forecasting has 
experienced a surge of interest in combination methods to 
enhance forecast performance. Numerous studies have dem-
onstrated the superior predictive ability of forecast combi-
nations in volatility forecasting (e.g., Becker and Clements 
2008; Christiansen et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2015; Zhang 
et al. 2019). For a recent extensive review on combination 
approaches, the reader is referred to the work of Wang et al. 
(2023). From simple regression techniques to more sophis-
ticated optimization strategies, most combination method-
ologies are based strictly on statistical criteria for allocating 
weights across individual forecasts.
Second, financial practitioners and investors are not only 
concerned with statistical accuracy but also prioritize the 
economic value of volatility forecasts. Evaluating volatility

ing option pricing, a utility function, and a risk manage-

evaluates volatility forecasts using various economic criteria 
(e.g., Bandi et al. 2008; Lyócsa et al. 2021; Lu et al. 2021; 
He et al. 2021).
Lastly, it has been established in prior research that superior 
performance in terms of statistical loss functions, such as the 
mean squared error, does not necessarily translate into eco-
nomic gains (see, e.g., Cenesizoglu and Timmermann 2012; 
Bernales and Guidolin 2014; Andrada-Félix et al. 2016). By 
introducing a time-varying combination scheme where weights 
on individual models are assigned based on the past perfor-
mance of each model in economic terms, we aim to bridge the 
gap between statistical accuracy and economic value.
The importance of selecting and evaluating volatility 
estimates and forecasts in the context of the application for 
which the forecast is required has been highlighted in several 
studies (e.g., Elliott and Timmermann 2008; Andrada-Félix 
et al. 2016). In the financial forecasting literature, numerous 
studies evaluate the predictive ability of alternative fore-
casting techniques in an asset allocation application. In the 
context of stock return predictability, Campbell and Thomp-
son (2008) and Rapach et al. (2016) among others employ 
the certainty equivalent return (CER) for a mean–variance 
investor who allocates his budget between stocks and risk-
free bills. In the volatility forecasting literature, studies 
including Wang et al. (2016), Lyócsa and Todorova (2020), 
Zhang et al. (2021) compare CER computed using various 
volatility forecasts. Another strand of the literature on vola-
tility forecasting attempts to evaluate the usefulness of vari-
ous volatility forecasting methods in the context of option 
trading (see Angelidis and Degiannakis 2008; Andrada-Félix 
et al. 2016; Degiannakis et al. 2018; Ballestra et al. 2019; 
Wang et al. 2020). From another perspective, Degiannakis 
et al. (2013), Amendola and Candila (2016), Bams et al. 
(2017), Clements and Preve (2021), Ding et al. (2021) 
among others evaluate the ability of various volatility mod-
els to provide accurate VaR forecasts. Moreover, Fameliti 
and Skintzi (2020) evaluate the forecasting performance of 
various statistical combinations of volatility forecasts based 
on both statistical and economic loss functions.
Although the idea of decision-based evaluation of RV fore-
casts has become popular in the recent literature, an extremely 
limited number of studies have attempted to combine forecasts 
based on economic criteria. Pettenuzzo and Ravazzolo (2016) 
consider density combination forecasts where the combina-
tion weights depend on the past forecast performance of the 
individual models through a utility-based objective function. 
Caldeira et al. (2018) propose a forecast combination strategy 
in which model weights are based on the portfolio returns in 
the context of an optimal mean–variance bond portfolio prob-
lem. Taylor (2020) proposes the use of Value-at-Risk (VaR) and 
expected shortfall loss functions for estimating combination 
weights to predict VaR and expected shortfall. In this study, 
we contribute to the literature by employing three economic 
criteria that require volatility forecasts as inputs and include (a) 
the economic gains for a mean–variance investor who optimally 
allocates his wealth between the stock index and a risk-free 
asset, (b) the profits from an option straddle trading strategy, 
and (c) an asymmetric VaR-based loss function. We apply our 
proposed methodology for combining measures of S&P500 
realized volatility where combination weights are tuned to 
depend on the models’ past economic performance using three 
economic functions. Combinations based on economic criteria 
(named economic combinations hereafter) are compared with 
the individual models and combination methods based on sta-
tistical loss functions in an out-of-sample exercise.
Our results indicate that economic combinations can 
result in greater economic gains than their competitors in 
all three forecasting exercises. However, no single method 
of combining RV measures based on economic criteria is 
uniformly accepted as the best performer across all applica-
tions. Our results are robust to alternative sample sizes and 
volatility forecasting models, especially for the utility-based 
and option-based combination and evaluation strategies. We 
also examine the forecasting performance of our methodol-
ogy over longer forecast horizons, during periods of low and 
high volatility, during crisis periods, in international markets 
and in terms of statistical significance. Notably, economic 
combinations are extremely valuable in economic terms dur-
ing crisis periods and periods of high volatility. Moreover, 
the superior performance of economic combinations is sta-
tistically significant under a number of statistical tests.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec-
tion "Combination methods" presents the statistical combina-
tion methods and the novel economic combination techniques. 
Section "Empirical setup" outlines the data on the RV meas-
ures used in this study, describes the details of the forecast-
ing exercise, and outlines the statistical and economic criteria 
employed to evaluate and compare volatility forecasts. Section 
"Forecasting results" presents the empirical results. Section 
"Extensions" discusses several robustness checks followed 
by various extensions presented in Section "Conclusions". 
Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper, summarizing the find-
ings and outlining potential avenues for future research.

Standard combination methods
Our analysis considers several standard methods for com-
bining forecasts, which can be grouped into four catego-
ries based on the method used to determine the weights. 
The first category includes simple combination techniques 
that do not involve complex calculations. Despite their 
apparent simplicity, research has shown that these tech-
niques often outperform more complex methods (Stock 
and Watson 2004; Timmermann 2006; Smith and Wallis 
2009). The four methods we examine in this category are 
the mean, median, geometric mean, and trimmed mean 
combinations. The mean combination involves taking 
the equal-weighted average of all n individual forecasts, 
whereas the median and geometric mean combinations 
use the median and the geometric mean of the individual 
forecasts, respectively. The trimmed mean combination 
excludes the smallest and largest forecasts and assigns a 
weight of 1/(n-2) to the remaining forecasts.

forecasting performance, a vast body of literature on fore-

When estimating combination forecasts via a statisti-
cal loss function, a hurdle is the unavailability of the target 
variable, the latent quadratic variation, which necessitates 
the use of a proxy. To address this issue, we employ the 
approach suggested by Patton (2011), Patton and Sheppard 
(2009), and Cubadda et al. (2017) and use the squared daily 
open to close return as a proxy for the target variable. This 
proxy has been shown to be an unbiased estimator of the 
latent volatility measure (Liu et al 2015) and is not employed 
as a predictor in the individual models.
Economic combinations
Forecast combination is a well-established and well-tested 
approach for enhancing forecasting accuracy. However, 
the existing combination methods rely solely on statistical 
measures, whereas financial practitioners and forecasters are 
more interested in the economic value of volatility forecasts, 
as highlighted in previous studies (Wang et al. 2016; Ma 
et al. 2018). Nonetheless, it is unclear whether minimizing 
a statistical loss function, such as the Mean Squared Error 
(MSE), leads to significant economic gains as mentioned by 
Andrada-Felix et al. (2016).
To this end, we contribute to the combination forecast-
ing literature by proposing a novel approach that employs 
economic criteria to generate combination forecasts. The 
proposed methodology includes combination schemes based 
on economic performance measures. A notable advantage 
of our proposed method is that it does not require a proxy 
for the unobserved quadratic variation, a common limitation 
in traditional statistical methods. To evaluate the historical

forecasts from each individual model are estimated starting

Empirical setup
Realized volatility measures
This section begins by introducing several commonly uti-
lized realized measures, followed by a discussion on dif-
ferent methods for evaluating them. A diverse range of 
realized measures has been introduced in existing literature 
(Andersen et al. 2001, 2010, among others). The aim of this 
paper is to develop a combined estimator that surpasses the 
effectiveness of any individual estimator since each realized 
measure provides distinct and valuable information.
Our empirical analysis is based on a total of eight real-
ized volatility measures that correspond to the S&P 500 
index. The first two measures, denoted ­RV5 and ­RV10, are 
standard realized variance estimators based on 5-minute and 
10-minute frequency returns, respectively (Andersen et al. 
2001; Bollerslev et al. 2016). Additionally, we consider the 
realized kernel estimators introduced by Barndorff-Nielsen 
et al. (2009) using three different kernels, the non-flat Parzen 
­(RKParzen) estimator, the two-scale Bartlett (RKtwo-scale) 
estimator, and the modified Tukey-Hanning ­(RKTukey-Hanning) 
estimator. Finally, we examine three alternative realized vol-
atility estimators, namely the jump-robust bipower varia-
tion (BV) estimator (Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard 2006), 
the median (MedRV) estimator (Andersen et al. 2012), and 
the downside risk semivariance (SV) estimator (Barndorff-
Nielsen et al. 2010), all based on 5-minute frequency returns. 
Further details and analytical calculations are available in 
Shephard and Sheppard (2010).
The data span the period from January 1, 2000, to Octo-
ber 30, 2020. All data series are daily in frequency and were 
collected from the Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative 
Finance Realized Library (http://​reali​zed.​oxford-​man.​ox.​
ac.​uk/​data).
Forecasting approach
Τhis section outlines the design of our forecast experiment, 
which is similar to that adopted by Lyócsa et al. (2021). 
Specifically, we generate out-of-sample volatility forecasts 
using a rolling window methodology. The initial 1,000 
observations are used as the in-sample period, while the 
remaining observations form the out-of-sample period. 
Within the out-of-sample period, the first 500 observations 
are allocated to the calibration sample (CS) for computing 
combination weights, if required. The first forecast begins 
with the (1500+h)st observation. We opt for a rolling cali-
bration sample to enhance flexibility in the combination 
forecast procedure and ensure that the best single models 
are promptly included in the forecast pool.

Evaluation methods

Forecasting results
In this section, we present the results of our out-of-sample 
forecasting exercise. Specifically, we compare the statistical 
and economic performance of one-day ahead forecasts of 
quadratic variation, generated by single models, and statisti-
cal and economic combination schemes.
Statistical evaluation
To provide a comprehensive evaluation, we assess all the 
competing models using two statistical loss functions: the 
MSE and the QLIKE loss functions. We present the rankings 
and results of these evaluations in Table 1. The weighted 
option combination yields the lowest MSE, followed by the 
ΤW option and the 50% trimmed option combinations. The 
MCS test demonstrates that various combination models 
based on option strategy performance and statistical loss 
functions meet the criteria for selection according to the 
MSE criterion. Furthermore, the SPA test results indicate 
that option combinations outperform all other models. When 
considering the QLIKE loss functions, option combination 
forecasts are the best performers, and they are the only mod-
els to survive the MCS test. We note that the option com-
bination models are followed by the statistical combination 
models, whereas the Q loss- and CER-based combinations 
perform poorly in statistical terms. In sum, option combina-
tions are the best performers across both forecast metrics, 
highlighting their superiority in statistical terms.

suggest that during crisis events and high volatility periods, 
more sophisticated forecasting models focused on economic 
performance criteria prove to be particularly valuable. These 
models outperform their traditional counterparts and offer 
superior forecasting performance in economic terms.
International evidence
The empirical results presented in the previous sections 
focus on the US stock market volatility. We expand our 
analysis and investigate the predictive power of the proposed 
combination methods in three major stock markets, the UK, 
France, and Germany. Data on the international realized 
volatility measures are extracted from the same database as 
the US volatility measures, i.e., the Oxford-Man Institute 
of Quantitative Finance Realized Library. Tables 8, 9, and 
10 provide international evidence on the forecasting per-
formance of economic combinations based on three perfor-
mance measures. Across all countries, the best CER stands 
out as the clear winner in the asset allocation exercise. In 
the option trading exercise, the best option method performs 
exceptionally well for UK and France. In the case of Ger-
many, the 70% trimmed option combination outperforms 
the other models in forecasting stock market volatility and 
the best option is ranked second. In the risk management 
context, at least one of the economic combinations outper-
forms single and statistical combination forecasts, except for 
Germany, where the trimmed MSFE takes the top spot and 
the 70% trimmed Q ranks second. In summary, international 
evidence aligns with our previous findings, demonstrating 
that economic combinations yield the highest economic 
value.

Summary of results
The empirical results of this study encompass three differ-
ent economic loss functions, along with various extensions 
and robustness checks. Table 12 provides a comprehensive 
overview by presenting the best-performing models across 
the explored scenarios. Shaded cells highlight cases where 
an economic combination yields the best outcome. These 
findings clearly demonstrate that economic combinations 
generally outperform other models, particularly for asset 
allocation and risk management-based combinations, and 
during turbulent periods. The superior performance of 
economic combinations during high-uncertainty periods can 
be explained by their ability to adapt dynamically to chang-
ing conditions. Attaining economic gains or managing risk 
during such volatile times is challenging, as not all individ-
ual models can quickly adapt to sudden and rapidly changing 
conditions. Some models, like the BV model, which excels 
during stable periods, experience a severe decline in per-
formance during high volatility. Economic combinations, 
however, demonstrate a distinct advantage: they dynami-
cally identify and allocate greater weight to models that 
show strong recent economic performance while minimiz-
ing weights or even disregarding underperforming models
Conclusions
In this paper, we extend existing statistical combination fore-
casting strategies and allow them to depend on the past eco-
nomic performance of each forecast. Our main motivation is 
to demonstrate that combining forecasts based on a specific 
economic application can lead to additional economic gains. 
We employ our methodology in an out-of-sample forecasting 
exercise using various estimators of S&P500 realized volatil-
ity. Three economic criteria are used for combining and evalu-
ating forecasts: a utility function, an options straddle trading 
profit function and a risk management loss function. Although 
the ranking of the models change based on the economic cri-
teria used, we conclude that economic combinations consist-
ently outperform their competitors across all three economic 
applications. The overperformance of economic combinations 
is consistent under a number of robustness checks and exten-
sions, especially for CER-based and option-based combina-
tions. Interestingly, during extremely turbulent and high vola-
tility periods, incorporating economic combinations into the 
decision-making process yields superior out-of-sample gains 
for investors.
Overall, our study highlights the benefits of combining vola-
tility forecasts using economic criteria, taking into account the 
specific application context. By incorporating economic value 
into the combination process, our methodology offers improved 
forecasting performance with significant implications for prac-
titioners and investors in financial markets. Future research can 
explore additional combination schemes based on economic cri-
teria and examine the performance of economic combinations 
in different asset classes.

Abstract: We propose a forecast combination scheme that employs time-varying weights, which depend on the financial decision for which the forecasts are used. Combination weights are computed through three alternative economic performance meas- ures, a utility-based function, an option staddle trading strategy, and a risk management loss function. We apply our model combination approach to various realized volatility estimators of the S&P500 and compare the forecasting performance of the combinations based on economic criteria to that of a variety of existing combination methods based on statistical loss functions. The results imply that our proposed combination schemes result to superior economic performance compared with the individual measures and statistical combination methods. Our findings are supported by a wide range of robustness checks and extensions Moreover, the suggested combination framework holds significant economic value during times of crisis and high volatility.
